title: Relationship Degree
description: Distinguish relationship arity from row and column counts, preserve genuine ternary facts, and reject participant triples that are not supported by one complete assignment.
notes:
## Degree classifies the association structure

Relationship degree describes the participating entity categories in the introductory ER convention used here. A Student-Course enrollment is binary because it connects those two categories. A teaching assignment connecting Faculty, Course, and Semester is ternary. The classification concerns the association's conceptual structure, not how many current instances occur or how many descriptive attributes are stored in its mapped table.

Terminology needs care when one type appears in several roles. This lesson follows the common introductory description of a self-association as unary or recursive because one entity type participates. A Manages relationship still has distinct manager and subordinate roles. More formal role-based treatments can discuss arity differently, so make the convention explicit rather than presenting the word degree without its interpretation.

## Degree differs from cardinality ratio

A binary relationship can allow one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many participation under different domain requirements. Degree two does not mean exactly two relationship instances, exactly one child per parent, or one matching occurrence on each side for every record. The maximum multiplicities and minimum participation rules need their own specification.

For example, Student-Course enrollment can be many-to-many while Instructor-Office assignment might be one-to-one under a particular policy. Both can be binary in this convention. A current fixture with one matching pair does not establish either policy for every allowed state. Distinguish a conceptual participation constraint from the observed count of facts in a small dataset.

## Do not confuse relationship degree with relation degree

A relational table's degree counts its attributes. A mapped binary enrollment table can contain student_id, course_id, enrolled_on, and score, giving that relation four attributes. It still represents a binary Student-Course association in the selected ER convention. Descriptive relationship attributes do not automatically become additional participating entity categories.

Conversely, a ternary mapping can contain more than three columns because it stores relationship properties or implementation identity. Adding an internal assignment_id does not turn Faculty-Course-Semester into a four-participant conceptual relationship. Read the meaning and roles first, then separately count the SQL output or table attributes when that is the question being asked.

## Recursive roles remain distinguishable

Employee Manages Employee connects occurrences of the same category in manager and subordinate roles. The identifiers can appear in separate columns such as manager_id and subordinate_id. Their matching SQL types do not make the roles interchangeable. A reversed pair can express a different fact even when both employees exist in the same entity set.

Classifying the relationship as unary in this lesson does not imply only one identifier value is involved in an instance. Nor does it prove the graph is a tree, forbid self-management, or prevent longer cycles. Those are separate requirements. State the role-based association and its constraints before interpreting the classification label as a complete implementation design.

## Ternary facts bind three participants jointly

Consider Teaching(faculty_id, course_id, semester_id). One tuple means that a particular faculty member teaches a particular course in a particular semester. Faculty 1 teaching Course 10 in Semester 100 is a different fact from that faculty member teaching Course 10 in Semester 200. The semester identifies a participant in this model, not an unrelated label to ignore when comparing assignments.

A query seeking a specific teaching assignment must match all three roles. Matching only faculty and course can return an assignment from the wrong semester. Matching only course and semester can return a different faculty member. The complete triple carries information that is not contained in one arbitrary pair. Attribute and key choices should preserve the exact association required by the domain.

## Binary projections can lose joint information

Suppose the recorded triples are (1, 10, 100), (1, 20, 200), and (2, 10, 200). Their pair projections include faculty-course pair (1, 10), faculty-semester pair (1, 200), and course-semester pair (10, 200). Each of those pairs appears somewhere among the true records, but the joint triple (1, 10, 200) is not one of the recorded facts.

Joining all three pair projections can therefore manufacture that extra triple. The result is a spurious combination, not proof that Faculty 1 teaches Course 10 in Semester 200. This concrete counterexample explains why a genuine ternary relationship cannot always be replaced safely by three independent binary associations without additional constraints or structure preserving the lost joint meaning.

## Safe decompositions need evidence

Some relationships have dependencies that support an information-preserving decomposition, or a design can introduce an assignment entity to retain the joint identity and connect its participants. Those are deliberate modeling decisions. They should not be inferred merely because a two-column table looks easier to draw or because a particular fixture happens not to reveal an extra combination.

A lossless design must reconstruct the intended facts without adding false combinations or omitting true ones under its allowed-state rules. The analysis depends on the actual constraints. One successful reconstruction of one small sample is evidence about that sample, not proof of every future state. Preserve the original meaning while reviewing any proposed decomposition and its mapping.

## Map the joint occurrence explicitly

A straightforward ternary teaching relation can store the three required participant identifiers, with a combined key under a one-assignment-per-triple policy. Supported foreign keys can enforce appropriate participant existence separately. The composite key protects duplicate joint identity; it does not automatically select the domain's maximum multiplicity for every participant pair.

```sql
SELECT faculty_id, course_id, semester_id
FROM teaching_assignments
WHERE faculty_id = 1 AND semester_id = 200
ORDER BY course_id;
```

This query asks which courses the specified faculty member teaches in the specified semester. It preserves the actual joint records. It should not infer additional courses by joining unrelated pairwise membership observations. A report's predicate and output need to retain enough roles to explain exactly which association occurrence each result describes.

## Ternary constraints need precise wording

A requirement such as each course has one teacher can be ambiguous when semesters are involved. Does it mean one teacher per course for all time or one teacher per course-semester pair? A unique course_id declaration would enforce the first interpretation, while a suitable unique course_id and semester_id combination expresses another restriction. The relationship's degree alone chooses neither.

Likewise, repeating a faculty identifier across many triples can be valid. Every participating identifier need not be individually unique in the association relation. Use the intended combination and cardinality rules rather than imposing a primary key independently on every component. Valid repeated participation should remain possible where the domain permits it.

## Higher-degree relationships need clarity rather than avoidance

A relationship involving four relevant participant categories can be appropriate if the joint fact really needs all of them. Increasing degree can make roles and constraints harder to communicate, but it is not automatically a design error or an instruction to split the association into arbitrary pairs. An intermediate occurrence entity can help when it preserves a clearly defined event or assignment identity.

The right design depends on the questions and allowed states. A supplier delivering a part to a project on a specified contract can have a genuine joint meaning that pairwise facts do not capture. Review the participant roles, occurrence identity, and dependencies before deciding which representation is simplest while remaining faithful to the required information.

## Test joint meaning with counterexamples

Use triples whose pairs overlap across different records, including the spurious-combination example above. A request for a proposed assignment should succeed only if the complete triple exists. An exercise can report unsupported proposals without asserting that absent participant entities are valid or that any particular assignment is authorized. Existence of the joint fact is a focused question with its own scope.

The SQL fixtures demonstrate explicit ternary filtering and complete-triple validation over synthetic data. They do not certify every decomposition, native participant-reference rule, or exact provider behaviour. Relationship degree is useful when it helps readers understand the association's structure while keeping cardinality ratio, SQL attribute count, recursive roles, and information-preserving mapping as distinct questions.

questions.question_text: In the introductory ER convention used here, what does relationship degree classify?
options: The number of instances that can relate to each other
The participating entity categories, with self-associations described as unary or recursive in this convention
Whether participation is mandatory
The number of attributes on the relationship
questions.explanation: Distinguish this classification from role-based arity treatments and SQL relation attribute count.

questions.question_text: What is the degree of the relationship Enrolls_In, connecting Student and Course?
options: 1 (unary)
2 (binary)
3 (ternary)
It depends on the cardinality
questions.explanation: Two entity sets (Student, Course) participate, making it a binary (degree 2) relationship.

questions.question_text: In the introductory one-participating-type convention, how is an Employee self-association described?
options: A weak relationship
A recursive relationship, connecting an entity set to itself
An identifying relationship
A derived relationship
questions.explanation: The association is called unary or recursive here, while its two participant roles remain distinct.

questions.question_text: Which best distinguishes relationship degree from cardinality?
options: They are the same concept
Degree classifies association structure; cardinality ratio describes permitted participant multiplicities
Cardinality counts entity sets; degree counts instances
Degree only applies to binary relationships
questions.explanation: Neither is simply the current count of stored relationship instances.

questions.question_text: Why can a genuine ternary relationship like Teaches(Faculty, Course, Semester) NOT always be safely replaced by three separate binary relationships?
options: Because SQL forbids ternary relationships
Because splitting it can lose information about which specific triples of Faculty+Course+Semester are jointly valid
Because ternary relationships cannot have attributes
Because binary relationships are always faster to query
questions.explanation: Decomposing a true ternary association into pairwise binaries can allow reconstructing combinations that were never actually valid together, losing the original constraint.

questions.question_text: Is a binary relationship (degree 2) necessarily 1:1 in cardinality?
options: Yes, always
No — a binary relationship's degree is independent of its cardinality, which can be 1:1, 1:N, or M:N
Only if both entity sets are weak
Only in recursive relationships
questions.explanation: Degree (2, binary) says nothing about cardinality; these are separate dimensions of the relationship.

questions.question_text: Under this lesson’s introductory convention, what degree label describes Employee Manages Employee?
options: It cannot be determined
questions.explanation: One entity category participates in distinct manager and subordinate roles, so this convention calls it unary.

questions.question_text: Why should a relationship involving four relevant participant categories be reviewed carefully rather than split into arbitrary pairs?
options: They are forbidden by the ER model
The joint meaning and constraints can be harder to express, but any simplification must preserve the intended information
They can never have attributes
They automatically violate entity integrity
questions.explanation: Higher degree is not automatically wrong. An intermediate occurrence identity or justified decomposition can help when it preserves the actual facts.

questions.question_text: Does a binary relationship necessarily have one-to-one cardinality?
options: Yes; binary means exactly one on each side
No; degree and permitted multiplicity are independent
Only when names repeat
Only for empty sets
questions.explanation: A binary association can support several cardinality ratios.

questions.question_text: A binary enrollment table has four columns. What does four measure?
options: The number of entity categories always
The number of students
Its relational attribute count, not necessarily ER relationship degree
The maximum enrollments
questions.explanation: SQL relation degree and conceptual association degree differ.

questions.question_text: Why is (1,10,200) unsupported by true triples (1,10,100), (1,20,200), (2,10,200)?
options: Its individual values never occur
Its pairs are all absent
No recorded row binds that complete triple
Every semester must be globally unique
questions.explanation: Pairwise occurrence does not establish joint occurrence.

questions.question_text: What can joining all pair projections of a genuine ternary relation produce?
options: Only guaranteed true triples in every model
A new primary key automatically
A lossless result by definition
Spurious triples not present in the intended association
questions.explanation: The projections can lose joint constraints.

questions.question_text: Does one successful sample reconstruction prove a decomposition is always lossless?
options: No; allowed-state dependencies need analysis
Yes; every future state follows the sample
Only if sorted
Only if there are three rows
questions.explanation: Sample agreement is weaker than a general guarantee.

questions.question_text: What does an internal assignment_id change by itself?
options: It always makes every ternary relationship quaternary
An implementation identity, not the number of conceptual participant categories
It removes semester meaning
It creates all foreign keys
questions.explanation: Implementation columns and conceptual roles differ.

questions.question_text: Why keep manager and subordinate roles distinct?
options: Both positions always mean the same employee
All self-associations are undirected
Reversing participant positions can change the fact
Roles generate identifiers
questions.explanation: A repeated type can have different participation roles.

questions.question_text: Which rule could mean one teacher per course-semester pair?
options: Only unique course_id for all time
Every faculty_id globally unique in assignments
A result alias
An appropriate uniqueness condition over course_id and semester_id
questions.explanation: The relevant combination expresses the intended scope.

questions.question_text: Must every component of a teaching triple be individually unique?
options: No; repeated participation can be legitimate
Yes; each identifier occurs once forever
Only if there is a primary key
Only if it is numeric
questions.explanation: The joint identity differs from component uniqueness.

questions.question_text: What should guide a higher-degree representation?
options: A universal ban on more than two participants
Joint meaning, occurrence identity and allowed constraints
Only the shortest diagram
Only current row counts
questions.explanation: Clarity must preserve the required information.

questions.question_text: What does a complete-triple proposal audit establish?
options: All underlying entities are authorized
Every binary decomposition is safe
Whether the proposed joint assignment exists in the checked data
All provider foreign keys were tested
questions.explanation: The audit answers a focused joint-existence question.

questions.question_text: Which fixture best challenges incomplete pairwise validation?
options: One isolated true triple only
An empty diagram
Only unique course names
Overlapping pairs drawn from different true triples
questions.explanation: The counterexample exposes spurious joint inference.

coding_problems.title: Query a complete ternary teaching population
coding_problems.task: Return faculty_id, course_id and semester_id for assignments with faculty_id 1 and semester_id 200. Use the recorded triples, without inferring extra combinations from pairs.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE teaching_assignments (faculty_id INT NOT NULL, course_id INT NOT NULL, semester_id INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(faculty_id,course_id,semester_id));
constraints: Each stored triple is a distinct joint assignment; participant existence is assumed in these temporary fixtures.
edge_cases: A matching faculty-course pair in another semester is not enough.
The requested faculty can teach several courses in one semester.
hints: Keep all three identifying roles in the result.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT faculty_id, course_id, semester_id FROM teaching_assignments WHERE faculty_id = 1 AND semester_id = 200 ORDER BY course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The query retains the intended joint facts rather than treating individual pair appearances as proof of a complete assignment.

coding_problems.title: Reject unsupported joint teaching proposals
coding_problems.task: Return proposal_id, faculty_id, course_id and semester_id for proposed triples absent from teaching_assignments. A proposal whose three pair projections each appear somewhere still needs one matching complete assignment.
coding_problems.schema_sql:
CREATE TABLE teaching_assignments (faculty_id INT NOT NULL, course_id INT NOT NULL, semester_id INT NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY(faculty_id,course_id,semester_id));
CREATE TABLE proposals (proposal_id INT PRIMARY KEY, faculty_id INT NOT NULL, course_id INT NOT NULL, semester_id INT NOT NULL);
coding_problems.seed_sql: INSERT INTO teaching_assignments VALUES (1,10,100),(1,20,200),(2,10,200); INSERT INTO proposals VALUES (1,1,10,200),(2,1,10,100),(3,2,20,100);
constraints: Proposal identifiers distinguish submissions; repeated proposed triples can appear in separate submissions.
This checks joint membership, not production assignment authority or native participant-reference enforcement.
edge_cases: Pairwise-supported but jointly absent proposals must be reported.
Valid complete triples must be excluded from the error report.
hints: Match all three participant roles in the join.
Use a guaranteed nonmissing assignment component to test whether a full match exists.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT p.proposal_id, p.faculty_id, p.course_id, p.semester_id FROM proposals p LEFT JOIN teaching_assignments t ON t.faculty_id = p.faculty_id AND t.course_id = p.course_id AND t.semester_id = p.semester_id WHERE t.faculty_id IS NULL ORDER BY p.proposal_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The anti-join preserves the complete ternary meaning and exposes the classic spurious-combination case without constructing an unsafe decomposition.

validation_cases.seed_sql: INSERT INTO teaching_assignments VALUES (1,10,100); INSERT INTO proposals VALUES (1,1,10,100);

original_questions.question_text: What does the degree of a relationship measure?
options: The number of instances that can relate to each other
The number of entity sets participating in the relationship
Whether participation is mandatory
The number of attributes on the relationship
original_questions.explanation: Degree counts how many distinct entity sets are connected by the relationship (unary, binary, ternary, etc.).

original_questions.question_text: What is the degree of the relationship Enrolls_In, connecting Student and Course?
options: 1 (unary)
2 (binary)
3 (ternary)
It depends on the cardinality
original_questions.explanation: Two entity sets (Student, Course) participate, making it a binary (degree 2) relationship.

original_questions.question_text: What is a unary (degree 1) relationship also commonly called?
options: A weak relationship
A recursive relationship, connecting an entity set to itself
An identifying relationship
A derived relationship
original_questions.explanation: Unary and recursive relationship describe the same construct — an entity set related to itself, e.g., Employee manages Employee.

original_questions.question_text: Which best distinguishes relationship degree from cardinality?
options: They are the same concept
Degree counts entity SETS participating; cardinality counts how many entity INSTANCES on each side can be linked (1:1, 1:N, M:N)
Cardinality counts entity sets; degree counts instances
Degree only applies to binary relationships
original_questions.explanation: Degree is structural (how many sets), cardinality is numeric on instances (how many can link) — independent properties.

original_questions.question_text: Why can a genuine ternary relationship like Teaches(Faculty, Course, Semester) NOT always be safely replaced by three separate binary relationships?
options: Because SQL forbids ternary relationships
Because splitting it can lose information about which specific triples of Faculty+Course+Semester are jointly valid
Because ternary relationships cannot have attributes
Because binary relationships are always faster to query
original_questions.explanation: Decomposing a true ternary association into pairwise binaries can allow reconstructing combinations that were never actually valid together, losing the original constraint.

original_questions.question_text: Is a binary relationship (degree 2) necessarily 1:1 in cardinality?
options: Yes, always
No — a binary relationship's degree is independent of its cardinality, which can be 1:1, 1:N, or M:N
Only if both entity sets are weak
Only in recursive relationships
original_questions.explanation: Degree (2, binary) says nothing about cardinality; these are separate dimensions of the relationship.

original_questions.question_text: In the recursive relationship Manages (Employee manages Employee), what is the degree?
options: It cannot be determined
original_questions.explanation: Even though the same entity set plays two roles, only one distinct entity set (Employee) participates, giving degree 1.

original_questions.question_text: Why are relationships of degree 4 or higher rare in practice?
options: They are forbidden by the ER model
They quickly become difficult to design, query, and reason about, and are often decomposed using intermediate entities
They can never have attributes
They automatically violate entity integrity
original_questions.explanation: High-degree relationships are conceptually and practically unwieldy, so designers typically simplify them where possible.
